mainTopic: The barley-penalty story, then the משנה of two potters who trip: why the fallen one pays, and רבא's rule for a chain of falls
overview: This amud opens by finishing a story about date residue left in the public domain. The גמרא asks why רב הונא publicly declared someone's barley ownerless, when he holds we do not teach that rule publicly. It answers that those owners had been warned and ignored it, so this was a special קנס. Then a new משנה begins: two potters walk one behind the other, the first trips and falls, the second trips over him, and the first pays. רבי יוחנן says even the רבנן agree, because the first potter could have stood up and did not. רב נחמן בר יצחק says he pays even if he could not get up, because he should have warned the one behind him. The גמרא tries to prove רב נחמן בר יצחק's view twice, first from the beam-and-barrel משנה and then from a ברייתא about potters and glassmakers. Both proofs are pushed off. Finally רבא rules that the first person pays the second for damage from his body and his property, but the second pays the third only for damage from his body. The גמרא challenges this rule with a 'whichever way you look at it' question.

steps.title: The last word of the story: date residue
steps.stepSummary: The text opens with the last word of a sentence that began before this section: 'date residue!'
steps.whatsHappening: This one word finishes the story from the lines just before. It names the item that was left lying in the public domain, which was date residue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier lines told how public items left in the street were handled, and this word closes that sentence. Hold onto the picture: the waste was left where people walk, and it was treated as free for anyone to take. The next step builds on this story.

keyTerms.meaning: Date residue, the leftover pulp from dates (used as animal feed or fertilizer)
The public domain, a place where many people walk

steps.confusionAlert: Don't try to read this word alone as a full thought. It is only the end of a sentence that began before this section.

phrases.english: Date residue?!
phrases.notes: This word finishes the sentence from the lines just before. It's what was lying in the public street.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in the preceding lines of the daf, before this section starts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Completes the earlier remark about what was left in the public domain.

steps.title: Did רב הונא change his mind?
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה's public action fits his own view. But רב הונא said we don't rule this publicly, so did he retract?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רב אדא בר אהבה, since he acted according to his own ruling. But רב הונא, shall we say he changed his mind?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא compares two rabbis' actions with their own stated opinions. It finds that רב הונא's public declaration seems to contradict what he said earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אדא בר אהבה holds this is the הלכה and that we also teach it publicly, so acting publicly is no problem for him. רב הונא held that it is the הלכה but we do not teach it publicly. Yet he publicly declared the barley ownerless, which looks like a reversal.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / granted (one side fits fine, but the other is a problem)

phrases.english: It makes sense for Rav Adda bar Ahava
he acted according to his own ruling.
But Rav Huna,
shall we say he changed his mind?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה כִּשְׁמַעְתֵּיהּ אֶלָּא רַב הוּנָא לֵימָא הֲדַר בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the stories just told to question whether רב הונא's action fits his stated view.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's earlier position that this is the הלכה but we do not teach it publicly
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His public declaration that the barley was ownerless seems to be exactly the public teaching he said we don't do.

steps.title: The barley owners had been warned
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא did not change his mind. Those owners had been warned and ignored it, so he penalized them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רב הונא's action was a special penalty for people who had been warned, not a general public ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רב הונא would not publicly declare such items ownerless. Here the owners had been told to clear their barley from the street and refused. Making the barley ownerless was a קנס aimed at them, so his general opinion stays the same.

keyTerms.meaning: A penalty imposed by the court

steps.whatToRemember: רב אדא בר אהבה rules publicly that the item is up for grabs. רב הונא agrees it is the הלכה but does not teach it publicly. He only acted publicly as a קנס against people who were warned and refused.
steps.confusionAlert: מוּתְרִין here does not mean 'permitted' (from מותר). It comes from התראה, a warning, so it means 'they had been warned'.

phrases.english: Those people had been warned.
phrases.notes: He means the barley owners. They were told to remove their barley from the street and didn't.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: a special penalty for people who were warned, not a general public ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא's public declaration showed he now teaches the rule publicly.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב הונא kept his opinion. He acted only because these specific owners ignored a warning.

steps.title: משנה: Two potters, one trips over the other
steps.stepSummary: Two potters walk one behind the other. The first trips and falls, the second trips over him, and the first pays for the second's damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two potters were walking one after the other. The first tripped and fell, and the second tripped over the first. The first is liable for the second's damages.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new case. It deals with damage caused by a person who fell down in the public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first potter fell by accident, yet the משנה still makes him liable when the second potter trips over his body. This connects to the theme of the פרק, which is obstacles left in the public domain. The גמרא will soon ask why someone who fell without fault should have to pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: The case raises the basic question of whether a person who fell by accident is treated like a careless person whose body became a בור (a hazard) in the street.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Two potters
who were walking one after the other,
and the first tripped and fell,
and the second tripped over the first
the first is liable for the second's damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁנֵי קַדָּרִין שֶׁהָיוּ מְהַלְּכִין זֶה אַחַר זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the second potter trips over the first potter who fell, the first is liable for the second's damages.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: Liable because he could have stood up
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the משנה fits even the רבנן. Stumbling itself is an accident, but staying on the ground when he could have gotten up is his fault.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Do not think our משנה follows only רבי מאיר, who says that a person who stumbles is careless and must pay. Even the רבנן, who say a person who stumbles could not help it and does not pay, agree that here he pays, because he could have gotten up and did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by explaining whose view the משנה about the potters follows. רבי יוחנן says it fits everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the משנה matches only רבי מאיר, who blames anyone who stumbles. רבי יוחנן shifts the blame from the fall to what happened after it. The fall was an accident, but lying in the way when he could have stood up was his own fault.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who could not help what happened
Do not say; do not think

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן is not saying the רבנן hold that stumbling is careless. They still say the fall was an accident. He is only liable for not getting up afterward.
steps.whyThisMatters: This separates two moments: the accident and the failure to fix it. A person can be blameless for the first and still responsible for the second.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: לָא תֵּימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא,
phrases.english: Do not say that our mishnah is the view of Rabbi Meir,
who says: one who stumbles is negligent, and so he is liable;
rather, even according to the Rabbis,
who say he could not help it, and so he is exempt,
here he is liable,
since he could have stood up, and he did not stand up.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תֵּימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה of the two potters from step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even according to the רבנן, the first potter is liable because he could have stood up and did not.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: Liable because he could have warned
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק gives a different reason. Even if the potter could not get up, he should have warned the one behind him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Even if you say the first potter could not have stood up, he could have warned the one behind him, and he did not warn him.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different reason why the first potter pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the משנה makes him pay even when he truly could not get up. His fault is that he did not call out a warning. So by this view, the משנה covers more cases than רבי יוחנן allows.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא לֹא הָיָה לוֹ לַעֲמוֹד;
phrases.english: Even if you say he could not have stood up,
he could have warned, and he did not warn.
phrases.notes: He means warning the second potter walking behind him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא לֹא הָיָה לוֹ לַעֲמוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a broader reason than רבי יוחנן for the potter's liability
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first potter is liable even if he could not stand up, because he failed to warn.

steps.title: Why רבי יוחנן rejects the warning reason
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן holds that a person who cannot get up is too busy to warn anyone, so failing to warn is not his fault.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן would say: Since he could not stand up, he also could not warn, because he was busy trying to get up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבי יוחנן did not accept רב נחמן בר יצחק's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person struggling to get up is busy with that and cannot be expected to think about warning others. So for רבי יוחנן, the only real fault is not standing up when he was able to. That is why he limits the משנה to that case.

keyTerms.meaning: Because he is busy or preoccupied

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan says:
since he could not stand up,
he could not warn either,
because he was busy.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא הָיָה לוֹ לַעֲמוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי יוחנן's narrower reason against רב נחמן בר יצחק's broader one
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects failure to warn as an independent basis for liability
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Someone who cannot get up is busy and cannot be expected to warn others
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן: liable only for not standing up. רב נחמן בר יצחק: liable even for not warning. רבי יוחנן says a person struggling to get up is too busy to warn.

steps.title: The beam and barrel mishnah is brought as evidence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next משנה about a beam carrier walking ahead of a barrel carrier. It will use this to test the two views.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה: If the man carrying a beam walked first and the man carrying a barrel walked behind him, and the barrel broke against the beam, the beam carrier is exempt. But if the beam carrier stopped, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof. It quotes the beam and barrel משנה so it can test whether רב נחמן בר יצחק's view holds up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the man in front is not blamed when the one behind walks into him. But if he stopped suddenly, he pays. That raises a question the גמרא will take up next: does he pay simply for stopping, or because he stopped without warning?

keyTerms.meaning: The owner or carrier of the beam
The owner or carrier of the barrel

phrases.english: We learned in a mishnah:
If the owner of the beam was first
and the owner of the barrel was behind him,
and the barrel broke against the beam, he is exempt;
phrases.notes: The one who is exempt is the beam carrier walking in front.

phrases.english: but if the owner of the beam stopped, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a משנה to test the argument between רבי יוחנן and רב נחמן בר יצחק
steps.raayaObject: Whether רב נחמן בר יצחק's view, that failing to warn can make a person liable, is correct
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about the beam carrier and the barrel carrier

steps.title: The beam carrier stopped to shift his load, so his only fault was not warning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the beam carrier in the משנה stopped to shift his load, which is normal. He is still liable, so the reason must be that he failed to warn. This supports רב נחמן בר יצחק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't the משנה talking about a case where he stopped to shift the beam on his shoulder? That is normal for a carrier. Yet the משנה says he is liable, because he should have warned the person behind him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now uses the beam-carrier משנה from Step 8 to try to prove that failing to warn is enough to make someone liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stopping to shift a load is normal, so the stopping itself is not careless. If he is still חייב, the only fault left is that he did not warn the barrel carrier. That fits רב נחמן בר יצחק, who said failing to warn is the reason for liability.

keyTerms.meaning: to shift or adjust a load on the shoulder
it is his normal way; normal behavior

phrases.english: What, is it not that he stopped to shift his load on his shoulder,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the beam carrier walking in front of the barrel carrier, from the משנה in Step 8.

phrases.english: which is his normal way,
and yet it teaches that he is liable,
because he should have warned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the משנה quoted in Step 8 to support רב נחמן בר יצחק.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's view that failing to warn creates liability.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the beam carrier who stops and the barrel breaks against the beam.

steps.title: No, he stopped to rest
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The משנה may be talking about stopping to rest, which is not normal, so the stopping itself is his fault.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The משנה is talking about a case where he stopped to rest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading the משנה differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he stopped to rest, the person behind him could not have expected it. Then the stopping itself is careless, and the liability has nothing to do with warning. So the משנה no longer proves רב נחמן בר יצחק's point.

phrases.english: No, it is when he stopped to rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from Step 9 by changing the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof, not רב נחמן בר יצחק's view itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed he stopped to shift his load; the משנה could mean he stopped to rest.

steps.title: Then the משנה should have taught that stopping to shift is exempt
steps.stepSummary: If stopping to rest is liable and stopping to shift is exempt, the משנה should have taught that split inside its own case, instead of adding a later clause about saying 'Stop!'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he stopped to shift his load, what is the law, exempt? If so, instead of teaching in the last part, 'If he said to the barrel owner Stop, he is exempt,' the משנה should have made a split within the case itself: 'When is this said? When he stopped to rest. But if he stopped to shift his load, he is exempt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading from Step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה really meant only stopping to rest, then stopping to shift would be exempt. That would be an easy and natural split for the משנה to teach. Instead the משנה gives its exemption only for saying 'Stop!', which suggests stopping to shift is not exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: the last part of a משנה
let it make a split and teach
in what case is this said?

phrases.english: But if he stopped to shift his load, what? Is he exempt?
Instead of teaching in the last part:

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אָמַר לוֹ לְבַעַל חָבִית ״עֲמוֹד״ – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: 'And if he said to the barrel owner: Stop! he is exempt,'
let it split and teach within the case itself:
phrases.notes: Meaning within the first case of the משנה, the beam carrier who stopped.

phrases.english: When is this said? When he stopped to rest,
but if he stopped to shift his load, he is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל עָמַד לְכַתֵּף מַאי, פָּטוּר? אַדְּתָנֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'stopped to rest' reading from Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the משנה speaks only of stopping to rest.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If stopping to shift were exempt, the משנה would have taught that split directly instead of the later 'Stop!' clause.

steps.title: The משנה teaches that saying 'Stop!' exempts even one who stopped to rest
steps.stepSummary: The משנה chose the 'Stop!' clause to teach a bigger point: even when he stopped to rest, warning the barrel owner exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us something new: even though he stopped to rest, if he says to the barrel owner 'Stop!', he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and defends the 'stopped to rest' reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stopping to rest is the worse case, since it is not normal. The משנה wanted to show that even there, a warning removes his liability. That new point is why the משנה used the 'Stop!' clause instead of the split, so the proof for רב נחמן בר יצחק stays rejected.
steps.whatToRemember: The beam-carrier משנה does not prove רב נחמן בר יצחק's view. It can be read as stopping to rest, and the 'Stop!' clause teaches that a warning exempts even in that case.

phrases.english: This teaches us:
that even though he stopped to rest,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָאָמַר לוֹ לְבַעַל חָבִית: ״עֲמוֹד״ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: when he says to the barrel owner: Stop! he is exempt.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the משנה's wording as teaching a bigger new point.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'Stop!' clause seemed to show the משנה missed an easier split.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה chose the 'Stop!' clause to teach that a warning exempts even one who stopped to rest.

steps.title: A new proof from the potters and glassmakers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about people tripping one after another. It suggests they had no chance to get up, so their liability must come from not warning, which supports רב נחמן בר יצחק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: potters and glassmakers were walking in a line. The first tripped and fell, the second tripped over the first, and the third tripped over the second. The first pays for the second's damage, and the second pays for the third's. If they all fell because of the first, the first pays for everyone. If they warned each other, they are all exempt. Isn't this talking about people who had no chance to get up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof for רב נחמן בר יצחק, this time from a ברייתא about a line of potters and glassmakers who trip over each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the fallen person is חייב, but if he warned the others he is פטור. The גמרא suggests he had no time to get up, so getting up was not his fault. If so, the only reason left for his liability is that he did not warn, which is exactly רב נחמן בר יצחק's view.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not? It introduces the reading the גמרא wants to prove.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
The potters and the glassmakers
who were walking one after the other;
the first one tripped and fell,
and the second tripped over the first,
and the third over the second –
the first is liable for the damages of the second,
and the second is liable for the damages of the third.
And if they fell because of the first one –
the first is liable for the damages of all of them.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הִזְהִירוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה – פְּטוּרִין.
phrases.english: And if they warned each other – they are exempt.
What, is it not
a case where they did not have the chance to get up?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof (Steps 8-12) was pushed off, the גמרא tries a second source built the same way.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's view that a fallen person is liable for not warning, even if he could not get up
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the potters and glassmakers, read as talking about people who had no chance to get up

steps.title: Maybe they could have gotten up
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The ברייתא may be talking about people who did have time to get up but did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is a case where they had the chance to get up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading the ברייתא differently: these people did have time to get up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If they could have gotten up and did not, staying on the ground is their fault. Then the ברייתא's liability can be explained by that, and it no longer proves that not warning alone makes someone חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: No. It rejects the suggested reading.
To stand up, to get back on one's feet

phrases.english: No, it is a case where they had the chance to get up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading of the ברייתא proposed in Step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof only, not רב נחמן בר יצחק's view itself
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed they had no chance to get up, but the ברייתא can be read as people who could have gotten up and did not.

steps.title: Then the ברייתא should have split its own case
steps.stepSummary: If those who could not get up are exempt, the ברייתא should have said so inside its first case instead of adding a separate clause about warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if they did not have a chance to get up, what would the law be? Exempt? If so, instead of teaching in the last part, 'If they warned each other they are exempt,' it should have split its own case and taught: When is this said? When they could have gotten up. But if they could not get up, they are exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the pushback from Step 14 by asking about the ברייתא's wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to Step 14, someone who could not get up would be פטור. That is an easy, clear split, so the ברייתא should have written it directly into its first case. Instead it added a different clause about warning, which seems to show the split does not exist.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a ברייתא or משנה
Let it make the split and teach it within that same case
When is this said? It limits a rule to a certain case.

phrases.english: But if they did not have the chance to get up,
what would the law be? Exempt?
If so,
instead of teaching in the last part:

phrases.aramaic: אִם הִזְהִירוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: if they warned each other – exempt;
let it split and teach within that case itself:
When is this said –
phrases.notes: 'This' is the first part of the ברייתא, that the one who fell is liable.

phrases.english: when they had the chance to get up,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא הָיָה לָהֶן לַעֲמוֹד – פְּטוּרִין!
phrases.english: but if they did not have the chance to get up – they are exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם לַעֲמוֹד מַאי, פָּטוּר? אִי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the pushback of Step 14 by pointing to how the ברייתא was written.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in Step 14 that the ברייתא is about people who could have gotten up
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If people who could not get up are exempt, the simplest way to teach that would be a split inside the first case. Choosing a warning clause instead suggests no such split exists.

steps.title: The warning clause teaches a bigger point
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא chose the warning clause to teach that even people who could have gotten up are exempt if they warned the others.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it teaches us: even though they had the chance to get up, if they warned each other, they are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 15 and explains why the ברייתא used the warning clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא chose the warning clause because it teaches something new: even someone who was at fault for staying down is פטור once he warned. So the pushback from Step 14 holds, and the proof for רב נחמן בר יצחק falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us. It points to the new idea in a wording.

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs end the same way. The beam-carrier משנה is read as stopping to rest. The potters ברייתא is read as people who could have gotten up. In each, the warning clause teaches that a warning exempts even that worse case. Neither source proves רב נחמן בר יצחק's view.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us –

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּהָיָה לָהֶן לַעֲמוֹד,
phrases.english: that even though they had the chance to get up,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הִזְהִירוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה – פְּטוּרִין.
phrases.english: when they warned each other – they are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question from Step 15 and so protects the pushback of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording: the ברייתא chose the clause that teaches the bigger new point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא should have taught the 'could not get up' split, so it must not believe in that split.
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning clause teaches more: even someone at fault for not getting up is exempt if he warned. The ברייתא gives no proof for רב נחמן בר יצחק.

steps.title: רבא's rule for the first and second person in a chain of falls
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that the first one who tripped pays the second for damage from both his body and his property. The second pays the third only for damage from his body.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The first person is liable for the second person's damages, both damage caused by his body and damage caused by his property. The second person is liable for the third person's damages caused by his body, but not damage caused by his property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new rule for the case of people tripping one after another. The first person's liability is wider than the second person's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא splits damages into two kinds: damage from the person's own body falling, and damage from his things, like the barrel he was carrying. The first person pays for both kinds. The second person, who tripped over the first, pays only for damage from his body. The rule is stated without a reason, and that sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage caused by his body, from the person himself falling.
Damage caused by his property, such as his barrel or the things he was carrying.
The first, second and third people in the chain of falls.

steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between the first and second person is what the גמרא will now attack. The challenge only works because רבא treats the two people differently.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: רִאשׁוֹן חַיָּיב בְּנִזְקֵי שֵׁנִי –
phrases.english: Rava said: The first is liable for the damages of the second –

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בְּנִזְקֵי גוּפוֹ, בֵּין בְּנִזְקֵי מָמוֹנוֹ.
phrases.english: both for damage by his body and for damage by his property.
The second is liable for the damages of the third –

phrases.aramaic: בְּנִזְקֵי גוּפוֹ, אֲבָל לֹא בְּנִזְקֵי מָמוֹנוֹ.
phrases.english: for damage by his body, but not for damage by his property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רִאשׁוֹן חַיָּיב בְּנִזְקֵי שֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the chain-of-falls ברייתא discussed in steps 13-16 and adds a new rule about what kinds of damage each person pays for.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first person who trips pays the second for both body damage and property damage. The second pays the third only for body damage.

steps.title: Either way, רבא's split does not seem to work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that רבא's rule cannot stand. Tripping is either negligence or it is not, and neither answer fits treating the first and second people differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it: If one who trips is negligent, the second should also be liable for everything! If one who trips is not negligent, even the first should be exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא with a two-sided question. Neither option seems to explain why the first person pays more than the second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Option one: tripping counts as negligence. Then the second person, who also tripped, should pay for his property damage too. Option two: tripping is not negligence. Then the first person should not pay anything either. Either way, the difference between the first and second person looks impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it; a challenge showing that both options lead to a problem.
Negligent, careless in a way that makes him responsible.

steps.confusionAlert: Both the first and the second person are a נִתְקָל, since each of them tripped (the first on the road, the second over the first). So whatever we decide about a נִתְקָל, negligent or not, should apply to both of them the same way.

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it?
If one who trips is negligent –
the second should also be liable!
phrases.notes: He means liable for everything, including the property damage that רבא said the second does not pay.

phrases.english: If one who trips is not negligent –
even the first should also be exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly attacks the rule רבא just gave in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's distinction between the first person, who pays for body and property damage, and the second person, who pays only for body damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided attack. If tripping is negligence, both people should pay for everything. If it is not negligence, neither should pay. There seems to be no middle ground that allows treating them differently.
